newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb jury continues penalty phase.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb jury continues penalty phase.

text.p: Jurors deciding the fate of convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh resume deliberations on Friday to determine whether he should be executed or spend the rest of his life in prison for the biggest mass murder in U.S. history.

When federal Judge Richard Matsch sent the jurors home on Thursday after the first day's deliberations during the penalty phase of the trial, he told them to "put the matter at rest as best you can" before returning on Friday.
The jury of seven men and five women, which returned the conviction is also charged with deciding his punishment. It is expected to deliberate on Saturday if necessary.

Polls show Americans favour putting the 29-year-old Gulf War veteran to death by lethal injection for the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that killed 168 people and injured hundreds more.
In their deliberations the jurors must weigh aggravating factors such as the meticulous way McVeigh planned the bombing against mitigating factors like his lack of a criminal record.
But the judge also cautioned the jury that its decision was "not a mechanical process" and in the end they are the "conscience of the community."
In her closing argument prosecutor Beth Wilkinson told the jury: "It's time. It's time for justice."
McVeigh is a traitor who turned on his own citizens, she said. "He is no patriot. He is a traitor and deserves to die."
But defence attorneys pleaded with the jury to spare the life of the young man, whom boyhood friends described as a friendly and happy child and former army buddies as a model soldier.
"Tim McVeigh is going to die in prison, there is no doubt about that. The question is when will he die in prison, sooner or later?" chief defence attorney Stephen Jones told the jury.
"He is not a demon, though surely his act was demonic," Jones said in his closing statement.
The defence team has argued that McVeigh was deeply distressed by the deaths of about 80 members of the Branch Davidian cult in Waco, Texas in 1993 after a 51-day standoff with federal agents.

Jones hinted there could be more violence if McVeigh were executed, saying the jury could take a first step to restoring "domestic tranquility" by sparing his life. "It's time for this madness to end. It's time to reconcile," he said.

But when chief prosecutor Joe Hartzler took his turn to address the jury he jumped on Jones' suggestion. "Well, that strikes me as tantamount to almost a terrorist threat ... That is pure intimidation and I'm assuming each and every one of you on the jury has the courage to disregard that kind of blatant intimidation," Hartzler said.
Jones also hinted that the true story of the bombing will never be revealed if McVeigh is put to death. "Dead men don't tell tales," he told the jury solemnly.

While juries around the United States have shown a growing willingness to vote for the death penalty, the same has not been true in the state of Colorado, generally regarded as more tolerant than surrounding states.
